question: Why did iZotope build Nectar 5 so a producer can click a sung word to add an effect, and let an AI build the vocal chain?

rungs.question: Why does Moments turn a sung vocal into lyrics at all?
rungs.answer: So small, word-sized effects, such as a delay throw on the last word of a chorus, can be added by selecting the word instead of drawing automation. iZotope says these details tend to take an hour of automation tweaking; MusicRadar describes Moments as a way to add them without getting into automation across several plugins.

evidence.quote: Some of the best vocal details are tiny: a delay throw on the last word of the chorus, a harmony that shows up for one line, a reverse swell into the hook. They're also the ones that tend to take an hour of automation tweaking.
it’s a fast and intuitive way to spice up a vocal with effects without getting into the weeds with automation across multiple plugins.
There’s no hunting through the waveform for the right syllable and no juggling of automation lanes across several plugins: pick the words, pick the effect, and play it back.

counter.text: The word-click route rests on the transcript, and iZotope's manual says it can be wrong: "Transcription won’t always spell every word the way you would, especially in a sung vocal." The producer corrects words by hand. MusicRadar's account follows iZotope's framing closely and puts "industry-first" in quotation marks as iZotope's claim.

rungs.question: Why can a transcript replace the automation?
rungs.answer: Moments is an ARA plugin: it reads the whole recorded clip on the DAW's timeline, not only the audio playing at that moment. So it can transcribe the take on the computer and tie each word to its stretch of audio. Highlighting text selects that audio, and the effect is applied to just that part.

evidence.quote: (Moments is an ARA plugin, meaning that it can edit audio on the timeline directly, rather than working on a stream of real-time audio that’s coming in through the DAW’s playback.)
Moments works on audio clips through ARA, which lets it read the whole clip, not just the audio playing at the moment.

It transcribes your vocal right on your DAW's timeline, so you can highlight words the same way you'd select text in a document, nudge the edges with waveform handles, and add an effect to just that part.

counter.text: The route depends on the host. The manual says: "If your DAW loads Moments as an ordinary effect instead of an ARA extension, Moments can’t hear your audio and shows a notice." The release notes list six ARA hosts ("Nectar Moments ARA: Logic (Rosetta), Pro Tools, Cubase, Nuendo, Fender Studio Pro, Reaper") against fourteen DAWs and editors for Nectar 5 as a whole. Outside those hosts the automation route remains.

rungs.question: Why does Nectar 5 also hand the chain itself to an AI?
rungs.answer: The same aim as Moments, applied to set-up: cutting the time from a raw take to a finished-sounding vocal. Vocal Assistant listens to part of the vocal and builds a processing chain for it in one click, as a starting point. Nectar 5 adds Custom Flow to steer it with style, register, key and an a cappella reference.

evidence.quote: This AI-powered mixing tool listens to a portion of your vocal and designs a customized processing chain to match it.
Skip the setup. Just like magic. Vocal Assistant analyses your sound and builds a tailored processing chain in seconds. Now including new modules from Nectar 5.
Vocal Assistant listens to your vocal and sets up your whole chain for it, from EQ and compression to pitch correction and space.

counter.text: None found against what the Assistant does, within the seven saved pages. Neither site reports an independent test of its results: MusicRadar's line that it has "been calibrated to deliver superior results" restates the maker's claim, and iZotope's manual frames the output as a starting point: "Vocal Assistant’s chain is a starting point."

rungs.question: Why does Vocal Assistant set the chain it sets?
rungs.answer: By iZotope's manual, it listens for 8 seconds by default, then moves the vocal's EQ toward a target: a built-in one for the vocal's style and register, or an a cappella the producer loads. It sets thresholds on a fixed FET-into-Opto compressor chain. Only the maker describes the targets; MusicRadar confirms the reference option alone.

evidence.quote: Equalizer: a high-pass filter set for the voice’s register, and gentle bell bands that move your vocal’s tone toward its target: the built-in target for its style and register, or your reference.
Serial Compressor: the classic FET-into-Opto vocal chain, followed by a Limiter.
Here you can choose to disable certain modules, upload an a capella reference recording and adjust two macro controls that tweak the overall intensity and spaciousness of the results.

counter.text: None found that contradicts the manual, within the seven saved pages. The manual's "tailored" chain is partly fixed: the compressor order is the same FET-into-Opto chain each time, with only thresholds set for the vocal, and a spoken vocal gets no Dimension, Delay or Reverb.

rungs.question: Why are the built-in targets what they are?
rungs.answer: The sources do not say. iZotope states only that the Assistant is trained on pro vocal standards and has been retuned. No page read names the training data, whose vocals set the built-in targets, what counts as a pro standard, or what changed in the retuning.

evidence.quote: Trained on pro vocal standards and retuned for even better results, Vocal Assistant can set up your whole chain in one click.
Trained on pro vocal standards, it gives you a tailored starting point in seconds, so you can spend your time dialing in your own sound.

counter.text: None found; scope: the iZotope product page, launch post, release notes, the Nectar 5 manual's home, Moments and Vocal Assistant pages, and the MusicRadar article. None describes the training data or method.

landing.shows: Both features aim at the same thing: removing setup work from vocal mixing. Moments swaps automation lanes for selecting words in a transcript, which works because ARA gives it the recorded audio on the timeline. Vocal Assistant swaps building a chain by hand for one click. The Assistant steers each vocal toward built-in targets for its style and register, and what those targets were built from is not in any page read.
landing.open_question: If every vocal is nudged toward the same built-in target for its style and register, made from unnamed pro vocal standards, whose sound is a producer starting from?
